readerTitle: Why go abroad? Count what you get to reuse
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (만두 체인, 미용실 예약 소프트웨어) + 실제 연구 (Ghemawat의 해외 진출 가치 논의)
insight: 해외 진출의 좋은 이유는 '새 고객이 많다'가 아니라 '이미 만들어 둔 강점을 더 많은 시장에서 다시 쓸 수 있다'는 데 있다.
misconception: 국내 성장이 둔해지면 해외로 나가는 것이 자연스러운 다음 단계다. 시장이 커지면 이익도 커진다.

sources.text: Ghemawat, P. (2007). Redefining Global Strategy: Crossing Borders in a World Where Differences Still Matter. Harvard Business School Press.
만두 체인과 예약 소프트웨어 회사는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Ghemawat(2007)가 해외 진출의 정당성을 '판매량 증가'만으로 판단하지 말고 비용 절감, 차별화, 위험 분산, 지식 축적 등 가치를 더하는 방식으로 따져야 한다고 주장한 내용(ADDING value scorecard)을 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체적 항목명과 약어를 쓰지 않고 일반적으로만 서술했습니다.
'많은 소프트웨어 회사가 일찍 해외로 나간다'는 문장은 일반적 관찰로만 썼습니다. 특정 통계는 넣지 않았습니다.
만두 체인(매장 12곳), 미용실 예약 소프트웨어 회사는 모두 가상 사례이며 수치는 설명용입니다.

cards.title: Two businesses, one plan, very different odds
body: A dumpling chain runs 12 busy shops in one country. A small software company sells booking tools to hair salons. Both have the same plan for next year: open in another country.
Both give the same reason. Growth at home is slowing. That turns out to be the weakest reason either of them has.

image.label: A dumpling shop and a laptop both looking at a world map
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 김이 나는 만두 가게, 오른쪽에 미용실 예약 화면이 뜬 노트북. 둘 다 가운데의 지도 쪽을 향해 있고, 지도 위 다른 나라에 작은 깃발. 실제 브랜드 로고나 국기는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which reason should carry the most weight?
body: You own the dumpling chain. Before you pay for a first shop abroad, your partners want one strong reason.

options.text: Sales growth at home has slowed, so we need new customers
options.feedback: It's true and it explains the urge. But it says nothing about why you would win abroad, where you start with no name and no regulars.

options.text: Our recipes, kitchen system and training took years to build, and they would work in a city that loves dumplings
options.feedback: This names what you bring with you. The more of your edge that crosses the border, the less you must rebuild from zero.

options.text: Two rivals just opened abroad, and we'll fall behind if we don't
options.feedback: Copying a rival's move feels safe, but their reasons may not be yours. You take on the cost without knowing what advantage you carry.

cards.title: What crosses the border, and what doesn't
body: Opening abroad means paying for some things a second time. The real question is how much you get to bring along for free.

breakdown.label: Recipes
breakdown.detail: Years of testing, reused at no extra cost

breakdown.label: Kitchen system
breakdown.detail: How a shop serves hundreds of orders an hour

breakdown.label: Training manual
breakdown.detail: New staff learn the same way everywhere

breakdown.label: Suppliers and name
breakdown.detail: New flour, new pork, and nobody knows you yet

cards.title: Transferable advantage
body: A good reason to go global is that something you already built, and already paid for, can earn money in more places. Call it a **transferable advantage**: an edge that still works after it crosses a border.

The chain's recipes and kitchen system cost the same whether they serve 12 shops or 40. Each new market spreads that cost thinner. A slow home market doesn't change this math. It only makes you want to believe it.

image.label: One recipe book feeding shops in three countries
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데에 두꺼운 레시피 책 하나, 화살표 세 개가 서로 다른 나라의 만두 가게 세 곳으로 뻗어 있음. 책에는 "Built once", 가게 쪽에는 "Used again" 라벨. 실제 국기와 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Software carries even more across
body: The booking company has a stronger version of the same case. Its product took years to build. Serving salons in a new country adds translation, local payment methods and support hours, but the core code is reused as it is.
This is why many software companies look abroad early. Most of their cost sits in building the product, not in delivering it. The dumpling chain, by contrast, must still build every new kitchen.

cards.title: "More customers" is rarely enough on its own
body: Strategy scholar Pankaj Ghemawat argues that a foreign move should be judged by how it adds value, not by how many sales it adds. Other reasons can be just as strong:
list: **Lower costs:** cheaper inputs or production elsewhere
**Follow your customers:** a supplier whose big clients open abroad
**Spread risk:** one country's slump hurts less
**Learn:** a demanding market teaches skills you bring home
cards.callout: Each good reason names what you gain, not just where you go.

cards.title: Some advantages don't travel
body: If customers love you for the owner's personality, one great location or a local reputation, that edge stays home. Abroad you'd be a newcomer without it.
And every move costs more than the plan says: new rules, new suppliers, a name nobody knows. Going global pays when the advantage you carry is bigger than everything you must rebuild.

image.label: A suitcase half packed, some items left behind
image.brief: 열린 여행 가방 일러스트. 가방 안에는 "Recipes", "System", "Code" 라벨이 붙은 물건. 가방 밖 바닥에 "Location", "Local fame", "Owner's charm" 라벨 물건이 남겨져 있음. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Now it's the booking software.
body: Your salon booking app is growing more slowly at home. Your product works well, and translation is cheap. How should you go abroad?

options.text: Launch in five countries at once to grow fast
options.feedback: You reuse the code five times, but you also rebuild support, payments and sales five times before learning whether the product really travels.

options.text: Pick one country where salons book and pay much like at home, and adapt only what's needed
options.feedback: You carry over the most and rebuild the least. You also learn what travels before spending more.

options.text: Wait until nearly every salon at home is a customer
options.feedback: You avoid foreign costs for now, but the product you paid for earns in only one market. A rival may take the next one first.

cards.title: Go abroad to stretch what you've built, not to escape a slow home market.
body: The best case for going global names the advantage you carry across the border and shows it is worth more than what you must rebuild.
**Try it today:** list the reasons customers choose you. Mark each one "travels" or "stays home". The "travels" list is your real case for going global.
